summary: This standards-track memo defines a set of SNMP managed objects for monitoring and managing DOCSIS-compliant cable modems and cable modem termination systems. It replaces RFC 2669. It was itself later updated by RFC 9141.

eli5.summary: Cable modems are like little machines with dials and gauges. This document lists the dials and gauges so a network operator can read them from far away.

questions: what is the docsis cable device mib
how do you upgrade cable modem software over snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects an operator reads and sets to manage DOCSIS cable modems and the CMTS equipment that serves them.

tldr.problem: Cable operators need a standard way to monitor and configure many DOCSIS cable modems (CMs) and cable modem termination systems (CMTSs) from afar.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DOCS-CABLE-DEVICE-MIB module, a set of SNMP managed objects covering basic device status, software upgrades, event reporting and notification throttling, and traffic filters.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2669, adds IPv6-capable objects and SNMPv3-era changes, and deprecates several older tables. RFC 9141 later updated it.

today: RFC 4639 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2669 and has since been updated by RFC 9141. Read the two together.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4639 defines a MIB module, a set of managed objects accessed with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), for DOCSIS-compliant cable modems (CMs) and cable modem termination systems (CMTSs). A CM acts as a slave station in a cable data system. A CMTS sits in the head-end, acts as the master station, is the only station that transmits downstream, and controls the scheduling of upstream transmissions by its CMs.

The specification is derived from the DOCSIS Radio Frequency Interface specification. DOCSIS 1.0 only required cable modems to implement SNMPv1 and to handle IPv4 customer traffic. DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 require SNMPv3 as well as SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, and this revision reflects that. The RFC notes that DOCSIS 3.0 and later are expected to require IPv6.

The MIB is written in SMIv2 and replaces RFC 2669.
sections.eli5: A cable company has thousands of modems in people's homes. This document is a shared list of the things you can check or change on each one, so every company asks in the same way.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organised
sections.content:
The module has seven components, each made of one or more groups. The base group extends the MIB-II system group with cable-device objects, plus groups for IGMP status and for the maximum number of customer devices (CPEs) allowed through a modem. Other components cover SNMP access control, software upgrades, provisioning-server progress, event reporting, filters, and CPE address control.

Several groups are marked deprecated in this version. The SNMP access groups are deprecated because of the SNMP coexistence work in RFC 3584. The older filter group is deprecated in favour of the LLC filter group and the Differentiated Services MIB (RFC 3289).

Most tables are specified not to persist across reboots. On reboot they are cleared and repopulated from the DOCSIS configuration file supplied by the cable operator, which lets a modem adapt to a new operator. The event table is the notable exception, kept for debugging.
sections.eli5: The list of dials is sorted into drawers: basics, security, software, events, filters. Some old drawers are marked 'do not use anymore' because better ones exist now.

sections.title: Software Upgrades and Event Reporting
sections.content:
To upgrade a modem's software from a management station, the operator sets docsDevSwServer to the address of the TFTP server, docsDevSwFilename to the image path, and docsDevSwAdminStatus to upgrade-from-mgt. A new object, docsDevSwServerTransportProtocol, lets the download use HTTP instead of TFTP. The device may refuse an upgrade if the download or file is incomplete or damaged, or the software is not meant for that hardware. A device that implements the BPI+ code verification checks signatures bundled with the image.

Events can be reported through syslog, notifications (traps and informs) and non-volatile logging. The MIB also lets an agent use the SNMP Notification MIB and the Notification Log MIB.

A CM and a CMTS MUST support notification throttling. The operator sets a measurement interval and a maximum number of notifications within it. In one rate-control method the device stops sending when the rate is exceeded and resumes only when a management station reactivates it. In the other it resumes when the rate falls back below the maximum. A separate limiting mode stops sending when a threshold is exceeded and resumes when the interval has passed.
sections.eli5: An operator can tell a modem 'go fetch new instructions from that computer'. The modem can also shout when something goes wrong, but you can tell it to stop shouting too much, like a smoke alarm with a limit on beeps.

sections.title: Filters on Traffic
sections.content:
The MIB includes link-layer (LLC) and IP filters. LLC filters can limit a modem to certain network-layer protocols such as IP, IPX, NetBIOS and AppleTalk, for example permitting only IP and ARP or dropping NetBIOS. IP filters can match source and destination addresses, transport protocols such as TCP, UDP and ICMP, port ranges and ToS values.

A cable modem applies filters in a set order: inbound LLC filters, then "special" filters, then inbound IP filters, then outbound IP filters, then any final outbound LLC filters. The special filters are IP spoofing filters, which discard packets from a CPE whose source address is not in the CPE tables, and SNMP access filters, which apply only to SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c traffic.

For IP filters, the table is scanned starting from the lowest-numbered filter. A matched row can drop the packet, accept it, or apply a set of policy actions, and a continue flag lets scanning go on to further filters. The IP filter tables are deprecated in favour of the Differentiated Services MIB.
sections.eli5: Filters are like a row of security guards at a door. The first checks what kind of visitor you are, the next checks you are using your own address, and so on, and any guard can turn you away.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 2669
sections.content:
The revision list in the RFC includes:

  • IPv4 address objects were deprecated and replaced or mirrored with IPv6-capable objects, for example the new docsDevCpeInetTable.
  • Objects made obsolete by SNMPv3 and the coexistence MIBs, such as docsDevNmAccessTable, were deprecated.
  • New objects: docsDevIgmpModeControl (passive or active IGMP operation), docsDevMaxCpe (maximum CPEs granted access) and docsDevSwServerTransportProtocol.
  • docsDevEvThrottleThresholdExceeded replaces docsDevEvThrottleInhibited.
  • Compliance statements were updated, with the CPE objects made optional and CM and CMTS requirements split.

The compliance statements still require only IPv4 addresses, because the DOCSIS versions then current were not IPv6 capable.
sections.eli5: This is the list of fixes from the last edition: new dials were added, some old ones were crossed out, and the rules were split for modems and for the big boxes at the cable company.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that the MIB relates to a system providing metropolitan public internet access, so improper changes could deny service to many users. Changing the access, filter and CPE tables could let a user raise his or her service level, spoof IP addresses or change the permitted management stations.

Specific risks it names include software download objects (an improper download may cause substantial vulnerabilities and loss of control of the modem), docsDevResetNow, unconstrained notification throttling that may flood traps, and syslog settings that could redirect sensitive information. Devices SHOULD implement BPI+ code verification for downloaded images.

It recommends blocking the tiny fragment and overlapping fragment attacks in IP filtering. SNMPv3 USM and VACM MUST be used with any v3 agent that implements this MIB module. Versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: If someone could change these dials without permission, they could cut off lots of neighbours or cheat the system. So only the cable company should be allowed to touch them, and with a proper lock.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The module uses one IANA-assigned object identifier value, recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: docsDevMIB is { mib-2 69 }. The RFC asks IANA for nothing else.
sections.eli5: The MIB gets one official number, 69, so nobody else uses the same spot in the big directory of network objects.

viz.caption: FILTER ORDER A CABLE MODEM APPLIES (RFC 4639)

items.title: 1. Inbound LLC
items.text: Level-2 frames entering from the RF side or a CPE interface.

items.title: 2. Special filters
items.text: IP spoofing filter, then SNMP access filter.

items.title: 3. IP filter in
items.text: Match, then drop, accept or apply policy.
